doc.title: Vince DiMartino interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, January 8, 2025

title: Bogota exchange semester and the dentist's office
summary: Sent to Colombia for free as a student, after shadowing a dentist, he sat in with a cumbia band at a hotel dance.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: Well I want to ask you, as a kid I had a couple of moments that really put me on a path, it was fortunate. And I read this anecdote about you had a semester away and you were in Bogota, Colombia.
I’d love to hear the details about this story.

It’s a good story because it really relates to my life choices. And that is, when I was in high school, you know I was a good student. And so you know that’s how I got to go to Bogota, the school sent me for free. And they sent another girl who was one of my good friends, she went to Guatemala. And I was sent to Colombia. They chose two students and for different reasons. I wasn’t the highest academic in the school, but I was up in the classes with those people. And so I went. I was getting ready — my dentist, who lived on the wealthy side of the street, the big street, you know he was a dentist. And his daughter was one of my best friends. We consulted on our homework at night you know. “Oh man, that trigonometry, that question number six did you —” you know and that kind of thing. “Did you get the answer to that? I kept getting this X — that ain’t it, you know what I mean?” And then we’d talk and I say, “Oh jeez, I missed that stupid decimal point, oh my

gosh.” But her dad was a dentist, okay? And you know I told him and I said, “Well you know I want to be either a doctor or a dentist.” You know I figured I want to live on that side of the street, that’s a pretty good place to be. So he said, “Well you can come over, and come to the office and you know see what I do.” So I went like once a week or once every two weeks, and I sterilized his stuff. Now they just throw it away and use new ones. But you know he had a sterilization thing and you put all the used instruments in there and then he can use them for the next patient or the next day or whatever. And he also gave me a nice white coat that I could watch what he was doing. And I wasn’t really excited you know about the stuff lying around in people’s mouth and everything. But I said well I can do this. I can probably do this. And I said well maybe I’ll go to a medical school and be a doctor. And I said well that’s not going to be any easier you know. So that was my junior year, and I went between my junior and senior year. And so I went down to Colombia. And it was about — I forget what the name of it — it was called the Open Door Exchange Program. And so you know there were about I don’t know, twelve, a dozen other students from different places on Long Island you know that went to the same place. And we had meetings and they took us on excursions. We went to Cartagena from Bogota and stayed about like two or three days and saw all the beautiful things there on the coast. But the family I was staying with, they had a sort of a — almost like a small cottage in the lowlands. Because Bogota is like about 7,000 feet up in the mountains. It’s about like Denver or something. And it rained there every day for about ten minutes and then it was absolutely gorgeous the rest of the time. And it was that way all year long. So they would take us down to the coast and they were kind of wealthy. There was a little country club there. And the place we stayed in was rustic at best. Spartan. I used to call it the “Spartan Arms” because you slept in a hammock in some of the rooms, and they had a swimming pool. The only thing that was there was they had their own swimming pool and they had this block, cement block cottage thing. And you could fit about five people in there and some of them sleeping in the living room. But the country club was great food and they had like traditional dancing there. So it was kind of neat. So after I’d been there a month man I wasn’t playing with anybody. I wasn’t doing anything. So there was a dance at this big hotel, the Hotel Tequendama. And it was a, you know at the time it was like “the” hotel so if your school had a dance they did it there because it was their big deal. And so I went and they had this cumbia band that played that music and I said, wow that’s really interesting stuff. I heard that on the radio and I said now I’m watching the musicians do this. And I told them I said, “Well I play trumpet you know.” So they said, “Well you can come back.” I said, “Well yeah, I played in the like All-State groups and stuff like that in America.” He says, “Well you can come back if you want to try to play with us.” So I did, I went back the next week and I played with them and they said,
